Floating-point addition is not associative because modern computers represent real numbers with finite precision. In exact arithmetic, the expressions (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) always have the same value. In floating-point arithmetic, however, each intermediate result is usually rounded to the nearest representable number. Changing the grouping changes which intermediate values are formed and rounded, so the final results can differ.

This effect is especially visible when numbers have very different magnitudes. If a very small number is added to a very large number, the small contribution may fall below the precision available at the large number’s scale and be rounded away. If several small numbers are added together first, their sum may become large enough to affect the larger value. Cancellation also matters: adding nearly opposite numbers can discard significant digits, making subsequent rounding errors more influential. IEEE 754 hardware defines floating-point formats and rounding behavior, but it does not make addition associative.

Matrix multiplication repeatedly computes dot products. Each output element is a sum of products, and a large matrix multiplication may require thousands or millions of terms per output value. A sequential implementation might accumulate these products from left to right. A parallel CPU implementation may split them among threads, compute partial sums, and combine those sums in a tree. A GPU may use a different tree based on thread blocks, scheduling, vector width, or optimized kernels. Distributed systems may combine partial results according to network timing or process topology. Although these methods evaluate the same mathematical sum, they create different intermediate sums and therefore different rounding errors.

The resulting discrepancies are usually small, often only a few units in the last place, but they can grow with long reductions, poorly scaled data, or severe cancellation. They may also propagate through later computations, especially iterative algorithms, threshold decisions, or nonlinear operations. Consequently, two matrix multiplications using identical inputs can produce slightly different bit patterns when run with different thread counts, hardware, libraries, compiler options, or reduction strategies.

Reproducibility therefore requires more than using the same floating-point type. Systems may need to enforce a fixed reduction order, use deterministic library modes, avoid timing-dependent accumulation, or employ more accurate summation techniques such as pairwise or compensated summation. Higher precision can reduce differences but does not restore associativity. Exact or reproducible accumulators can provide stronger guarantees, generally at a performance cost. Thus, high-performance matrix multiplication often trades strict bitwise reproducibility for parallelism and speed, while still aiming for results that remain acceptably close in a numerical sense.
